questions.question: List five conditions that make a site good for optical astronomy and explain how each helps. Explain why stars twinkle and what astronomers mean by 'seeing'.
questions.expected_answer: Darkness (no light pollution) lets faint objects stand out against a dark sky; clear skies with many cloudless nights; dry air with little haze or dust, since water vapour and dust absorb and scatter starlight; high altitude, so there is less air, moisture and dust above the telescope; steady air (good seeing) for sharp images; a clear view of the horizon; and a southern position to see southern objects such as the galactic centre and Magellanic Clouds. Stars twinkle because moving pockets of air at different temperatures bend their light by slightly different amounts from moment to moment; 'seeing' is the steadiness of the air, which determines how sharp telescope images are.

questions.question: Explain what light pollution is, give two of its harmful effects and two ways to reduce it. Explain how the Moon's phase affects observing and what interferes with radio telescopes.
questions.expected_answer: Light pollution is artificial light (streetlights, buildings, sports fields) that shines upward and scatters off particles in the air, making the night sky glow and hiding faint stars. Effects: wastes energy and money; hides the Milky Way from most people; harms wildlife (insects swarm, birds and sea turtles are confused). Reduce it with shielded fittings pointing downward, using only as much light as needed, warmer-coloured lights and switching off unneeded lights. Near full Moon, moonlight brightens the whole sky and hides faint objects, so new Moon is best for faint objects (though the Moon itself is a good target near first quarter). Radio telescopes are disturbed by radio interference from cellphones, radio and TV transmitters, aircraft, satellites and electrical equipment, so they are built in remote, legally protected radio-quiet areas.

questions.question: Name three South African observatory sites and explain why each was chosen. Describe how to prepare for a night of naked-eye stargazing.
questions.expected_answer: Sutherland (Northern Cape, SAAO observing station, home of SALT): about 1 800 m high, dry clear air, very dark skies far from towns, steady seeing and many clear nights; the main telescopes moved there from Cape Town in the 1970s because of city lights and winter cloud. The Karoo near Carnarvon (MeerKAT and SKA): remote, sparsely populated, protected radio-quiet zone with little radio interference. Hartebeesthoek (west of Johannesburg): a radio observatory in a valley where surrounding hills block interference from the city. (Also: SAAO headquarters in Cape Town, the old Royal Observatory founded 1820; Boyden Observatory near Bloemfontein, used for education and outreach.) Preparation: choose a clear night near new Moon; go to a dark, safe place away from lights; allow 20 to 30 minutes for the eyes to dark-adapt and avoid white light such as phone screens; use a red torch; take a star map or app in night mode and warm clothes; never look at the Sun.
